title: Euclid's Theorem on Infinitely Many Primes
subject: Number Theory
statement: There are infinitely many prime numbers: no finite list of primes can be complete, because another prime always lies beyond it.
short: Multiply your favourite primes and add one; some new prime must divide the result.
long: Euclid's argument does not hunt for a largest prime; it shows that no finite list can be complete. Any prime dividing N = p₁p₂···pₙ + 1 cannot be one of the listed primes, since it would then divide 1. The construction gives no estimate of how large the next prime is, but it works in astonishing generality across many number systems.
proof: Let N=p_1\cdots p_n+1>1 and let q be a prime divisor of N. If q=p_i then q divides N-p_1\cdots p_n=1, impossible; hence q is a new prime.
consequence: It is the starting point for every density question about primes and for Euclid-style proofs of infinitude in algebraic number fields.

title: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
subject: Number Theory
statement: Every integer greater than 1 factors into primes, and the factorisation is unique apart from the order of the factors.
short: Prime factorisations are the unique address of every integer — the reason primes are the atoms of arithmetic.
long: Existence follows by induction: if n is not prime, split it into smaller factors and repeat. Uniqueness is deeper, resting on Euclid's lemma that a prime dividing a product divides one of its factors. Without uniqueness, basic notions such as the greatest common divisor or the radical of an integer would be ambiguous.
proof: Existence by induction on n. For uniqueness, Euclid's lemma (p\mid ab\Rightarrow p\mid a or p\mid b) lets one cancel matching primes successively from two factorisations until both reduce to 1.
consequence: It underpins gcds and lcms, the arithmetic of rationals, and the system of valuations used throughout algebraic number theory.

title: Fermat's Little Theorem
subject: Number Theory
statement: For a prime p and any integer a not divisible by p, a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p); equivalently, a^p ≡ a (mod p) for every integer a.
latex: p\nmid a\Longrightarrow a^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p,\qquad a^p\equiv a\pmod p
short: Modulo a prime, raising to the p-th power changes nothing — a tiny observation with enormous reach.
long: The nonzero residues mod p form a group under multiplication. Multiplying them all by a merely permutes the list, so the two products are congruent and cancelling leaves a^(p−1) ≡ 1. The alternative form a^p ≡ a also covers the case where p divides a.
proof: The map x\mapsto ax permutes the nonzero residues mod p when p\nmid a, so (p-1)!\equiv a^{p-1}(p-1)!\pmod p; cancel since p\nmid (p-1)!.
consequence: It gives fast modular exponentiation tests, seeds Euler's theorem, and is the elementary backbone of public-key cryptography.

title: Euler's Theorem
subject: Number Theory
statement: If a and n are coprime positive integers, then a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n), where φ(n) counts the integers up to n coprime to n.
short: Fermat's little theorem for any modulus: the exponent is simply the number of invertible residues.
long: The reduced residue classes mod n form a group of order φ(n), Euler's totient. Lagrange's theorem says that any group element raised to the group order returns the identity. Setting n equal to a prime p gives φ(p) = p − 1 and recovers Fermat's little theorem; the general version is the workhorse of RSA.
proof: Multiplication by a permutes the \varphi(n) reduced residues mod n, so their product P satisfies P\equiv a^{\varphi(n)}P\pmod n. Cancelling the invertible P gives the claim.
consequence: It justifies RSA encryption and decryption and extends Fermat's theorem from prime moduli to arbitrary ones.

title: The Chinese Remainder Theorem
subject: Number Theory
statement: Congruences modulo pairwise coprime numbers always have a common solution, and that solution is unique modulo the product of the moduli.
latex: x\equiv a_i\pmod{m_i},\ \gcd(m_i,m_j)=1\ (i\ne j)\Longrightarrow x\ \text{unique mod}\ \prod_i m_i
short: Independent residue choices at coprime moduli combine into one integer, with no collisions.
long: The classical problem asks for a number leaving prescribed remainders when divided by 3, 5 and 7; because the moduli share no factors, exactly one answer exists modulo 105. In algebraic language, the theorem identifies Z/(m₁m₂···mₖ) with the direct product of the rings Z/mᵢZ, so arithmetic can be done one prime power at a time.
proof: Let M=\prod m_i and M_i=M/m_i. Since \gcd(M_i,m_i)=1, choose t_i with M_i t_i\equiv1\pmod{m_i}. Then x=\sum a_i M_i t_i works; two solutions differ by a multiple of every m_i, hence of M.
consequence: It enables fast modular computation by splitting a large modulus into small pieces and is the prototype of local-to-global reasoning in number theory.

title: Wilson's Theorem
subject: Number Theory
statement: An integer n > 1 is prime if and only if (n − 1)! ≡ −1 (mod n).
short: A factorial congruence characterises primes exactly, though far too slowly to be a practical test.
long: For a prime p, every residue from 1 to p − 1 pairs with its multiplicative inverse, and only 1 and −1 are their own inverses; the full product is therefore −1. Conversely, if (n − 1)! ≡ −1 mod n, any divisor d with 1 < d < n would divide the factorial but could not divide −1. The result is an exact criterion for primality, not an efficient one.
proof: In (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^\times, pairing each element with its inverse leaves only \pm1, so (p-1)!\equiv-1\pmod p. If n is composite with 1<d<n dividing n, then d\mid(n-1)! but d\nmid -1.
consequence: It gives a theoretical primality test, a neat way to compute factorials modulo primes, and an early link between group theory and elementary arithmetic.

title: Quadratic Reciprocity
subject: Number Theory
statement: For distinct odd primes p and q, the Legendre symbols (p/q) and (q/p) agree unless both primes are 3 mod 4, in which case they differ.
short: Two seemingly unrelated questions about square roots are tied together by the primes' residues mod 4.
long: The Legendre symbol records whether a number is a square modulo an odd prime. Gauss called the reciprocity law the golden theorem and gave several fundamentally different proofs. It converts the scattered question of which numbers are quadratic residues into a fast computation, and its structural explanation eventually required class field theory.
proof: Gauss's lemma relates (p/q) to the parity of the number of residues q,2q,\dots,((p-1)/2)q exceeding p/2; counting a lattice rectangle from both sides yields the exponent (p-1)(q-1)/4.
consequence: It makes quadratic residuosity efficiently computable, underlies probabilistic primality tests, and opens the door to higher reciprocity laws.

title: Dirichlet's Theorem on Arithmetic Progressions
subject: Number Theory
statement: If a and m are coprime positive integers, the progression a, a + m, a + 2m, … contains infinitely many primes.
latex: \gcd(a,m)=1\Longrightarrow p\equiv a\!\pmod m\ \text{for infinitely many primes }p
short: Primes reach every residue class that is not ruled out by a common factor — no admissible progression runs dry.
long: Progressions with gcd(a,m) > 1 are doomed because every term shares a factor with m. Dirichlet proved that this is the only obstruction, introducing characters and the non-vanishing of L(1, χ) at s = 1. His analytic method founded analytic number theory, and its quantitative refinement assigns about 1/φ(m) of all primes to each admissible class.
proof: Dirichlet characters split the problem: the principal character gives a divergent \sum_p 1/p, while nonprincipal ones stay bounded near s=1 because L(1,\chi)\ne0. Hence every admissible class contains infinitely many primes.
consequence: It guarantees primes in prescribed congruence classes for constructions in cryptography and coding theory and launched the study of L-functions.

title: The Prime Number Theorem
subject: Number Theory
statement: The number of primes at most x is asymptotic to x / ln x; equivalently, the nth prime is asymptotic to n ln n.
short: Primes thin out in a remarkably regular way: near x their density is about 1 / ln x.
long: Conjectured by Gauss and Legendre and proved independently by Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin in 1896, the theorem says the prime counting function π(x) approaches x / log x with relative error tending to zero. Both original proofs depend on the Riemann zeta function having no zeros on the line Re(s) = 1. Elementary proofs exist, but analytic methods give sharper error terms.
proof: Express \pi(x) through the von Mangoldt function as a contour integral of -\zeta'(s)/\zeta(s); shifting past the pole at s=1 and using the zero-free region on Re(s)=1 leaves the main term x.
consequence: It quantifies how common primes are, anchors probabilistic models of the primes, and drives estimates throughout analytic number theory.

title: Bertrand's Postulate
subject: Number Theory
statement: For every integer n > 1 there is a prime p with n < p < 2n: gaps between primes never outrun doubling.
short: There is always a prime between any number and its double — a weak but surprisingly useful guarantee.
long: Bertrand verified the claim numerically to a large bound; Chebyshev proved it analytically in 1850, and Erdős found an elementary proof in 1932 by estimating the central binomial coefficient. The result is much weaker than the prime number theorem, but strong enough for many arguments that merely need some prime in a controlled interval.
proof: Chebyshev's bounds on \pi(x) force \pi(2n)-\pi(n)>0 for n beyond a finite bound, with the remaining cases checked directly. Erdős replaced the analytic estimates by an elementary bound on the binomial coefficient \binom{2n}{n}.
consequence: It guarantees primes in short intervals, supports greedy arguments about prime gaps, and motivates stronger open questions such as primes between consecutive squares.

title: Unique Factorisation Fails in Z[√−5]
subject: Number Theory
statement: In Z[√−5], 6 = 2·3 = (1 + √−5)(1 − √−5): all four factors are irreducible, and the units ±1 cannot match the two factorisations.
short: A familiar integer acquires two incompatible prime decompositions once you enlarge the number system.
long: The norm N(a + b√−5) = a² + 5b² rules out any further factorisation of 2, 3 and 1 ± √−5, and the only units are ±1, so the two decompositions are genuinely different. Dedekind restored order by replacing elements with prime ideals: the ideal generated by 6 factors uniquely even though the elements do not. This is the classic warning that unique factorisation is a property of rings, not of numbers.
proof: N(2)=4, N(3)=9 and N(1\pm\sqrt{-5})=6; since a^2+5b^2 never equals 2 or 3, none of these elements has a proper factor. The only units are \pm1, so 2 is not associate to 1\pm\sqrt{-5}.
consequence: It motivated the invention of ideals and Dedekind domains, and explains why unique factorisation of ideals rather than elements is the right invariant for number fields.

title: The abc Conjecture
subject: Number Theory
statement: For every ε > 0, only finitely many triples of coprime positive integers a + b = c satisfy c > rad(abc)^(1+ε) — and this remains an unproven conjecture.
short: A simply stated bound tying sums to the primes inside them — famously deep, and not a theorem.
long: The radical rad(n) is the product of the distinct primes dividing n. The conjecture says that for each ε > 0 only finitely many coprime triples a + b = c have c larger than rad(abc) raised to 1 + ε; the extremal cases are sums where a and b consist of small primes repeated many times. It would imply strong forms of Fermat's Last Theorem and many Diophantine finiteness results, but no proof has been universally accepted.
proof: No proof exists: this is an open conjecture. Heuristic support comes from the fact that the quality log c / log rad(abc) is near 1 for typical triples, while triples of unusually high quality are extremely rare.
consequence: It would unify a large family of Diophantine finiteness statements and give effective control over solutions to many polynomial equations.

title: The Möbius Inversion Formula
subject: Number Theory
statement: If g(n) is the sum of f(d) over all divisors d of n, then f(n) is the sum of μ(d)g(n/d) over the same divisors.
short: A cumulative divisor sum can be undone exactly, using a function built from squarefree divisors.
long: The Möbius function μ(d) is zero when d has a squared prime factor and (−1)^k when d is a product of k distinct primes. Inversion recovers individual values from their divisor sums and is the arithmetic analogue of inclusion–exclusion. It also gives a clean proof that the reciprocal of the zeta function has μ(n) as its nth coefficient.
proof: \sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)=\delta_{n,1}, so swapping the order of summation gives \sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)g(n/d)=\sum_{e\mid n}f(e)\sum_{d\mid n/e}\mu(d)=f(n).
consequence: It recovers φ(n) from the identity ∑ over divisors of n of φ(d) equals n, and underpins Dirichlet convolution and the arithmetic of zeta functions.

title: The Lucas–Lehmer Test
subject: Number Theory
statement: For an odd prime p, 2^p − 1 is prime iff iterating x ↦ x² − 2 from x = 4 reaches 0 modulo 2^p − 1 after p − 2 steps.
short: A single recurrence decides the primality of a Mersenne number without any trial division.
long: The test is a deterministic criterion tailored to numbers of the form 2^p − 1 with p prime. Each step is one squaring modulo M_p, so the computation stays fast even when the number has millions of digits. It is how virtually every record large prime has been found, and its simplicity conceals a neat argument about finite fields.
proof: For prime M_p, 3 is a quadratic nonresidue, so \alpha=2+\sqrt3 lies in \mathbb{F}_{M_p^2} with norm 1 and order M_p+1=2^p. The recurrence gives s_k=\alpha^{2^k}+\alpha^{-2^k}, which vanishes at k=p-2; running the argument modulo any prime divisor of M_p forces that divisor to be M_p itself.
consequence: It powers the search for record Mersenne primes and shows how a special form can admit an exact, remarkably fast primality test.
